title: Brakes grinding
h1: Why do my brakes grind when I stop?
metaDesc: Grinding noise when braking? Answer a few quick questions to see if it's worn-out pads, rust, debris or a sticking brake, how urgent it is, and what to do next.
intro: A grinding brake ranges from harmless morning rust to pads worn down to bare metal. How the car stops, and when you hear the noise, tells them apart. Answer the questions below to see how urgent it is and what to do next.
safety: If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or the car takes longer to stop, stop driving and get help.
If the red brake warning light is on, don't drive until the brakes are checked.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, pull over safely and let it cool. Don't keep driving.

q_stopping.q: How does the car stop when you brake?
q_stopping.help: This is the most important question. A change in how the car stops matters more than the noise itself.

opts.a: Normally. Only the noise is new
It takes longer to stop, the pedal feels soft or goes lower, or the red brake light is on
It pulls hard to one side, or a wheel smells hot or burning
The pedal or steering wheel shakes or pulses along with the grinding

q_when.q: When do you hear the grinding?

opts.a: Only on the first few stops after the car sat, or after rain or a wash, then it's gone
Every time I brake: a harsh metal-on-metal grind
A light scraping that comes and goes, often after driving on gravel
Even when I'm not braking, and it changes with speed or when turning
Only during a hard stop or on a slippery road, with a buzzing pulse in the pedal
It started right after new brakes were put on

result.title: The brakes may not be working properly. Treat this as a safety problem
result.now: Don't drive it. Park it somewhere safe and have it towed, or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, use a lower gear if you can, and pull over somewhere safe.
If you see fluid near a wheel or the brake fluid reservoir is low, tell the shop. Low fluid with no visible leak still needs checking before the car is driven.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: Grinding plus longer stops or a soft pedal can mean the brakes have lost some of their ability to stop the car. Pads worn to metal, a fluid leak or a damaged caliper can all do this, and it can get worse suddenly.

causes.name: Pads worn through to metal
causes.clues: There was a squeal for weeks or months before the grinding started.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: A soft or sinking pedal, the red brake light, or a wet spot near a wheel.

causes.name: Damaged caliper or piston
causes.clues: Badly worn pads let the piston push out too far, and the pedal changed suddenly.

you: With the engine off and cool, check the brake fluid reservoir level.
Look for wet spots on the inside of the wheels.

result.title: A brake may be stuck on and overheating
result.now: Pull over safely and let the wheel cool. Don't touch it. Have the car towed or have a mechanic check it where it's parked before using it again.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone out and at least 100 feet away from the car and call for help.
If the parking brake was left partly on, release it fully and let the brakes cool. Overheated brakes can lose grip, so have them checked before relying on the car.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, don't drive it.
result.why: A brake that won't release can keep grinding against the rotor. That builds a lot of heat, which causes the burning smell and the pull, and it can make the brakes fade or damage the wheel bearing.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter or dustier, and the car pulls to that side.

causes.name: Parking brake not releasing
causes.clues: The heat is at a rear wheel.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The pull comes and goes.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Notice which wheel smells hotter from a distance. Don't touch it.

result.title: The brake discs may be worn or damaged, often along with the pads (rotors)
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal feels soft, sinks or the car takes longer to stop, don't drive it at all.
If the pulsing only happens during a hard stop on a slippery road, with no grinding on normal stops, it may be the ABS working. Mention it to the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: A pulsing pedal means the rotor surface is uneven. Combined with grinding, that can mean the pads have worn into the rotor or the rotor is badly rusted or scored. Metal-on-metal contact can reduce braking and gets worse with every stop.

causes.name: Pads worn into the rotor
causes.clues: Grinding on most stops, and a squeal before it started.

causes.name: Uneven or rusted rotors
causes.clues: The car sat for a long time, or the rotor has a rough ring or lip on its surface.

causes.name: Sticking caliper
causes.clues: One wheel gets hotter than the others.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the rotor surface. Deep grooves or a rough surface point to damage.
Notice whether the shake is in the pedal or the steering wheel.

result.title: Probably surface rust on the rotors scraping off
result.now: Brake gently a few times. If it's surface rust, the noise usually clears within the first few stops.
if: If the grinding lasts beyond the first few miles, have the brakes inspected soon.
If the car sat for weeks or months, have the rotors checked. Heavy rust can pit them.
If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or the grind is harsh, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: Brake rotors are bare iron and rust quickly when wet. After rain, a car wash or sitting overnight, the first stops scrape that rust off, which can sound like a brief grind. A brief grind that clears within a few stops is usually this.

causes.name: Light surface rust
causes.clues: Only on the first stops after the car sat or got wet, and gone soon after.
causes.against: If it happens on every stop all day, look for another cause.

causes.name: Heavier rust from long storage
causes.clues: The car sat for weeks, and the rotor edges look crusty.

you: Notice whether the noise is gone after the first few stops.
Look at the rotors through the wheel spokes for a shiny surface after driving.
shop: Rotor inspection if the noise doesn't clear

result.title: The brake pads may be worn down to bare metal
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop, or have a mechanic inspect the brakes where it's parked.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, leave plenty of room, and pull over somewhere safe. Then call for help.
If the pads were replaced recently and the grind started suddenly, a pad may have come apart. It still needs checking before you drive.
result.why: A harsh grind on every stop often means the pad lining is gone and the metal backing is rubbing the rotor. That can cut braking ability and damage the rotor quickly. Waiting can also damage the caliper.

causes.name: Pads worn through
causes.clues: There was a squeal for a while before, and the pads haven't been replaced in a long time.
causes.against: Less likely if the pads are new.

causes.name: Pad lining separated from its backing
causes.clues: The grind started suddenly on fairly new pads.

causes.name: Seized caliper wearing one pad unevenly
causes.clues: The noise is from one wheel, and that wheel runs hotter.

you: Look through the wheel spokes. If you can't see any pad material between the metal plate and the rotor, the pads are likely worn out. Tell the shop what you saw.

result.title: A small stone or bit of debris may be caught in the brake
result.now: Drive slowly in a safe place and back up a short distance. That often frees a trapped stone. If the scraping continues, book a brake check.
if: If the scraping becomes constant or turns into a harsh grind, have it checked right away.
If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or the brakes feel different in any way, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Small stones can get caught between the rotor and the thin metal dust shield behind it, causing a scraping sound that comes and goes. It often stops once the stone falls out, but it can score the rotor if it stays, so have it checked if the sound continues.

causes.name: Stone caught between the rotor and the dust shield
causes.clues: Started after gravel or a dirt road, and the noise is light and on and off.

causes.name: Bent dust shield touching the rotor
causes.clues: Started after a tire change or hitting something.

causes.name: Early pad wear
causes.clues: The pads are getting old, and a squeal came first.

you: Notice which wheel the sound comes from.
Look behind the wheel for a stone or a bent metal shield.
shop: Remove the wheel and check the rotor and dust shield

result.title: Possibly a wheel bearing, a dragging brake or a shield rubbing
result.now: Have it checked within a few days. Drive gently and avoid highways until then.
if: If the wheel feels loose, the steering suddenly feels different, or the noise gets louder fast, stop driving and have it towed.
If one wheel is hot or smells burnt, a brake is sticking. Don't drive it.
result.why: A grind that happens without braking and changes with speed or turning is less likely to be normal pad contact. It's often a worn wheel bearing, a brake that isn't fully releasing, or the dust shield rubbing the rotor.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: A grinding or growling that gets louder with speed and changes when you turn one way.

causes.name: Brake dragging
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter or dustier than the others.

causes.name: Dust shield rubbing the rotor
causes.clues: A light scraping that started after a tire change or hitting something.

you: Notice whether the noise changes when you gently turn left vs. right at speed.
Notice if one wheel smells hot after a drive. Don't touch it.
shop: Wheel bearing play and noise check

result.title: That may be the anti-lock brakes (ABS) doing their job
result.now: If it only happens during hard stops or on slippery roads, it's usually the ABS working as designed. Keep firm pressure on the pedal when you feel it.
if: If the buzzing happens during normal, gentle stops on dry roads, or the ABS light comes on, have the brakes checked.
If the car doesn't slow down as it should, or the pedal feels soft, stop driving and have it towed.
If the red brake warning light comes on, don't drive until the brakes are checked.
result.why: During a hard stop or on ice, rain or gravel, the ABS pulses the brakes rapidly so the wheels don't lock up. You can feel a buzz in the pedal and hear a grinding or chattering sound. That's how ABS is designed to work.

causes.name: Normal ABS operation
causes.clues: Only during hard or slippery stops, with a pulsing pedal.
causes.against: Not normal if it happens on dry roads during gentle stops.

causes.name: Faulty wheel speed sensor
causes.clues: The ABS kicks in at low speed on dry roads, or the ABS light is on.

you: Notice whether it only happens on slippery surfaces or in hard stops.
Watch for the ABS warning light.
shop: ABS code scan if it happens during normal stops

result.title: New brakes shouldn't grind. Something may need adjusting
result.now: Call the shop that did the work and arrange for them to recheck it within the next day or two. Drive gently and leave extra stopping room until then.
if: If the pedal feels different or the car takes longer to stop, don't drive it. Call the shop and ask them to come to you or arrange a tow.
If you smell burning or a wheel is much hotter than the others, stop and let it cool. Ask the shop to come to you or arrange a tow.
result.why: A little noise while new pads bed in can happen, but a true grind usually points to a fitting problem: a pad not seated right, a shield bent during the job, or old rotors with a worn lip that new pads are hitting.

causes.name: Pad or clip not seated correctly
causes.clues: The grind started right after the job and is constant.

causes.name: Old rotors not replaced or resurfaced
causes.clues: Only the pads were changed.

causes.name: Dust shield bent during the repair
causes.clues: A light scrape, even when not braking.

you: Check the invoice to see whether rotors were replaced.
Note which wheel it comes from.

result.title: Treat grinding as a brake problem until it's checked
result.now: Don't drive it until the brakes are inspected. Grinding can mean the pads are worn down to metal, and stopping can get worse quickly. Have it towed, or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or the grind is harsh on every stop, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If it was only on the first stop or two after rain, it may just be rust. Still mention it at the inspection.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, pull over and let it cool. Don't keep driving.
result.why: Grinding has harmless causes, like surface rust, but it's also the classic sign of pads worn to metal. Without knowing when it happens, it's safest to have the pads and rotors looked at quickly.

causes.name: Pads worn to metal
causes.clues: There was a squeal before, and the pads are old.

causes.name: Surface rust
causes.clues: Only after the car sits or gets wet.

causes.name: Debris or a bent shield
causes.clues: A light scrape after gravel or a tire change.

you: Record a short video with sound when it happens. It helps the shop.
Look at the pads through the wheel spokes.
